text: Welcome to Chapter Nine — cloud warehouse SQL dialects. We're leaving the classic on-premises OLTP world behind for a few lessons and looking at how SQL shows up in modern cloud data warehouses, starting with Snowflake. Here's the mental anchor to carry through this whole lesson: Snowflake's SQL is heavily ANSI-standard, and in most ways it actually reads closer to PostgreSQL than to T-SQL. When you're not sure what Snowflake does, guessing 'the standard option' will serve you better than guessing 'whatever T-SQL does.'

First difference you'll hit immediately: T-SQL's TOP has no Snowflake equivalent at all. Snowflake uses LIMIT instead — the same keyword PostgreSQL and MySQL use. Select top 10 product name, list price, order by list price descending becomes select product name, list price, order by list price descending, limit 10. The LIMIT clause goes at the very end of the query, not right after SELECT the way TOP does.

Second difference: concatenation. T-SQL overloads the plus sign to glue strings together — first name plus space plus last name. Snowflake uses double pipe instead, the ANSI-standard concatenation operator: first name, double pipe, space in quotes, double pipe, last name. If you try plus on Snowflake expecting string concatenation, you'll get arithmetic behavior or an error instead, not the result you want.

Third, and this one is a real trap for anyone used to T-SQL: case folding. T-SQL identifiers are case-insensitive but preserve exactly the case you typed. Snowflake identifiers are also case-insensitive by default, but get folded to UPPERCASE internally — the same family of behavior as Oracle. Select star from customers, Customers, or CUSTOMERS all resolve to the same uppercase object underneath. But quote an identifier — double-quote Customers — and now it preserves the exact case AND becomes case-sensitive. That's the exact same trap that catches developers moving from T-SQL to Oracle, and now you know it catches Snowflake too.

Now something genuinely new and genuinely useful: the QUALIFY clause. In T-SQL, filtering on a window function's result means wrapping the whole query in a CTE first, then filtering in an outer SELECT. Snowflake skips that entirely: select customer id, order id, row number over partition by customer id order by order date descending as rn, from orders, QUALIFY rn equals 1. One clause, no wrapping needed. Nothing in T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, or PostgreSQL offers this exact shortcut — it's distinctly Snowflake's.

One more Snowflake-specific feature worth knowing by name: Time Travel. Using AT or BEFORE clauses, you can query a table exactly as it existed at a past point in time — by offset, like 24 hours ago, or by an exact timestamp. There's no T-SQL equivalent to point to here; it's a genuinely distinctive capability of the platform. Next lesson, we go deeper into Snowflake's other standout feature: the VARIANT type for semi-structured data, and the dot-notation syntax that goes with it.
